title: Encoder overhead & telemetry: latency vs $ sensitivity lab notes
summary: Working notes from a small lab comparing client-side payload encoders (json, msgpack, protobuf) and transport compression (gzip, brotli) for chat and embedding workloads. Focus: how encoder choice and telemetry tags affect observed latency percentiles and cost-per-1M-tokens for hosted use-cases. Contains microbench numbers, ascii sparkline comparisons, open questions and suggested follow-ups.
body:
Context and motivation:
- We get repeated reports that certain customers see worse p95/p99 than our internal benches. One hypothesis: client encoders / telemetry payloads (long metadata fields, heavy JSON) increase request serialization/deserialization work and network bytes, which interacts with fast-path scheduling and causes extra queuing.
- Quick lab to: (1) quantify delta across encoders/compression; (2) surface where cost increases appear (client CPU, network, server decode time, alignment with batching windows); (3) rough $$ impact per 1M tokens.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Models: r-infer-3b-v1-slim (short seq workload) and r-infer-70b-v1 (long-decoder heavy)
- Workloads: chat-turns (avg 120 req tokens, 50 gen tokens) and embedding-batch (batch size 64, 512-dim)
- Client encoders: JSON (compact), JSON (pretty/verbose with meta), MessagePack, Protobuf-lite (schema with optional telemetry fields)
- Transport compression: none, gzip-6, brotli-4
- Telemetry envelope sizes: small (6 fields, 200B), medium (12 fields, 1.2KB), large (dynamic user context, 8KB)
- Repeats: 10k requests warm-started, 30k steady-state samples per cell

Micro-observations (raw):
- Network bytes (median per request, chat-turns, r-infer-3b):
  - JSON-compact / none: 1.8KB
  - JSON-verbose / none: 3.6KB
  - MessagePack / none: 1.4KB
  - Protobuf / none: 1.1KB
  - JSON-compact + gzip6: 520B
  - JSON-verbose + gzip6: 620B
  - Protobuf + gzip6: 480B
- Server-side observed decode CPU (median request CPU-ms):
  - JSON-compact: 0.85ms
  - JSON-verbose: 1.6ms
  - MessagePack: 0.6ms
  - Protobuf: 0.45ms
- Client serialization CPU (median):
  - JSON-compact: 0.95ms
  - MessagePack: 0.7ms
  - Protobuf: 0.6ms
- p50/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end, ms) for chat-turns, r-infer-3b, small telemetry envelope, no compression:
  - JSON-compact: p50 48ms, p95 82ms, p99 180ms
  - Protobuf: p50 46ms, p95 76ms, p99 160ms
  - JSON-verbose: p50 49ms, p95 95ms, p99 260ms
- Same workload + gzip6: p50 shift -2 to -4ms, p95 -5 to -12ms, p99 -20 to -40ms (relative improvements larger for verbose JSON)

Text-sparklines (p99, normalized to JSON-compact=no-compression baseline = 1.00):
- JSON-compact: 1.00
- Protobuf: 0.89 (sparks: ▁▂▁▁▃)
- MessagePack: 0.95 (sparks: ▁▁▂▁▁)
- JSON-verbose: 1.44 (sparks: ▁▇▇▇)
- JSON-verbose + gzip6: 0.92 (sparks: ▁▂▁▁)

Cost sketch (hosted token-dollar model, simplified):
- Assumptions: decode CPU adds 0.1% to per-token GPU time for 3B model, 0.6% for 70B; network egress cost $0.09/GB; CPU amortized cost per request negligible at infra scale (but impacts latency SLO which drives extra provisioning). We estimate incremental billing from network and tail-latency driven fallback/reserve capacity.
- Example delta for 1M chat-turns (small telemetry): extra bytes from JSON-verbose vs protobuf ~2.5KB per request => 2.5GB additional egress => ~$0.22 extra. Tail latency increase (p99 delta ~100ms) causes us to provision an extra 2% headroom for critical customer SLAs => amortized extra infra $40–$120 / month depending on instance sizing.
- Bottom-line: pure network $ impact is small for most cases (<$1k / month at 1M req/day), but latency-induced headroom/provisioning is the dominant cost vector for high-SLA tenants.

Where the encoder interacts with our runtime scheduling:
- Larger payloads push request arrival times across batching window boundaries. For low-latency windows (8–20ms fast-paths) even 200–500us of extra client encoder time can move a request to next batch, increasing p99 by one extra token-generation step.
- Verbose telemetry increases variance; that variance shows up heavily in p99 (not p50) because batching is sensitive to tail of arrival-time distribution.

Open findings / hypotheses to validate:
- H1: Telemetry size correlates much more strongly with p99 than with CPU decode time alone. Need ablation that modulates only the client-side serialization time (instrument client) vs payload bytes.
- H2: Compression (gzip/brotli) reduces p99 for verbose formats more than it hurts client CPU on modern mobile; test with mobile-phone emulators.
- H3: For embedding-batch workloads, protobuf + light compression reduces total egress by ~25% and improves slot packing which reduces cost-per-embedding by ~6% in our benches.

Immediate actionable recommendations (short):
1) Add a guide to SDKs recommending MessagePack/Protobuf for high-SLA customers and include a short code snippet in each SDK. (Owner: devx)
2) Default gzip for requests over 2KB on the hosted ingress layer; provide opt-out. (Owner: platform-ing)
3) Add telemetry-size alerting in Console: p95 payload bytes / p99 payload bytes per route, and correlate with p99 latency. (Owner: console/observability)
4) Run a targeted mobile/edge bench to measure client CPU vs compression tradeoff (Owner: eng-platform, due 2028-04-15)

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Run ablation where only serialization CPU is increased (busy loop) to test batch boundary sensitivity.
- Summarize a two-slide customer-facing one-pager explaining why big telemetry increases tail latency and modest monthly billing. Use simple visuals: "small telemetry" vs "large telemetry" p99 bars + $ delta.
- Investigate whether our ingress decompression step is blocking on main thread in some language SDKs (earlier slack thread from Marco suggests Go handler had sync decompress).

Appendix: sample request traces (simplified) showing batch boundary slips:
- Trace A (protobuf): arrival offset 3.2ms -> queued into batch @8ms window -> decode start 8.3ms -> gen start 9.0ms -> total 48ms
- Trace B (json-verbose): arrival offset 4.0ms -> missed 8ms window due to 0.9ms serialize -> queued into next window @16ms -> decode start 16.1ms -> gen start 17.0ms -> total 160ms p99 case

References / links back to artifacts:
- GH PR with a PoC gzip middleware: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2874
- Jira ticket to add payload-size metrics: JIRA-ENG-1423
- Slack thread: slack:#console-tooling~threads/CK12345 (key customer repros attached)

Quick conclusion (draft):
- Encoder choice and telemetry verbosity materially affect tail latency through a mix of network bytes and request arrival timing. For customers with strict p99 SLOs, recommend compact binary encoders or server-side gateway compression and adding payload-size telemetry to console. The raw dollar impact of egress is often small vs the provisioning cost driven by tail-latency headroom.

-- Aisha
